chemicals.concentration_notes: ◦ Distribution: The toxic alkaloids are found in the leaves and the fruits (berries). ◦ Potency: Ingestion can cause a wide range of severe clinical signs, from gastrointestinal distress to fatal circulatory collapse.
chemicals.description: ◦ Gastrointestinal Irritation: The alkaloids act as potent irritants to the gastrointestinal tract, capable of causing severe inflammation and hemorrhagic diarrhea (bloody stool). ◦ Systemic Neurological and Cardiac Effects: The toxins affect the central nervous system and heart, leading to progressive weakness, paralysis, and bradycardia (dangerously slow heart rate).
chemicals.name: Solanocapsine (and related alkaloids)

description:
Jerusalem Cherry (Solanum pseudocapsicum), also called winter cherry, is an ornamental nightshade plant with bright red or orange berries. It is toxic to cats, and the berries are the most tempting part.

The plant contains glycoalkaloids such as solanine and solasonine. These chemicals can irritate the digestive tract and may also affect the nervous system. All parts are unsafe, but the colorful berries create the highest household risk.

A cat that eats Jerusalem cherry may vomit, have diarrhea, drool, seem sleepy, act confused, or become weak. More serious cases can involve tremors or breathing problems. Keep the plant away from cats, and call a veterinarian if your cat eats any berries or plant material.
name: Jerusalem Cherry
safetyNotes: Toxic compounds: solanine and solasonine (steroidal glycoalkaloids); berries are most concentrated, but leaves and stems also contain toxins
Mechanism: glycoalkaloids inhibit acetylcholinesterase and disrupt cell membranes, causing GI and neurological effects
Symptoms: drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, lethargy, weakness; more severe ingestion may cause tremors, confusion, or bradycardia
The berries resemble small tomatoes or ornamental peppers and are visually appealing to cats
Keep Jerusalem Cherry out of cat-accessible spaces; contact your vet if berry ingestion occurs

symptoms.name: Vomiting, Diarrhea (often Hemorrhagic), Abdominal Pain, Anorexia
symptoms.notes: The diarrhea is specifically noted to be hemorrhagic (containing blood) in some cases. The irritation can also cause hypersalivation (drooling).Neurological Dysfunction (Seizures and Paralysis)
symptoms.onset: 2–24 hours (General onset for Solanaceae/Nightshade alkaloid toxicity).

symptoms.name: Convulsions (Seizures), Progressive Weakness, Paralysis, Dilated Pupils
symptoms.notes: The clinical picture includes progressive weakness that can escalate to paralysis and convulsions. The alkaloids affect the central nervous system significantly.
symptoms.onset: Delayed (Neurological signs often follow gastrointestinal distress as the toxin is absorbed).

symptoms.name: Bradycardia (Slow Heart Rate), Circulatory Collapse
symptoms.notes: The alkaloids can cause a dangerous slowing of the heart rate (bradycardia) leading to total circulatory collapse (shock).

symptoms.name: Dyspnea (Difficulty Breathing)
symptoms.notes: Respiratory paralysis or distress is a potential complication of the severe neurological depression caused by the toxin.

treatments.description: The veterinarian inserts a tube into the cat's stomach to wash out contents and remove unabsorbed plant material.
treatments.name: Gastric Lavage (Stomach Pumping)
treatments.notes: This is explicitly suggested to remove the toxic alkaloids from the system before they can be fully absorbed.

treatments.description: A substance is administered orally to bind with the remaining toxins in the gastrointestinal tract, preventing them from entering the bloodstream.
treatments.name: Administration of Activated Charcoal
treatments.notes: This step typically follows decontamination to minimize the bioavailability of the ingested alkaloids.

treatments.description: Intravenous (IV) fluids and electrolytes are administered to correct dehydration and imbalances caused by severe vomiting and diarrhea.
treatments.name: Fluid and Electrolyte Therapy
treatments.notes: This treatment is crucial for managing circulatory collapse (shock) and hemorrhagic diarrhea, both of which are potential severe symptoms of Jerusalem Cherry poisoning.

treatments.description: Medications are given to control or prevent seizures and convulsions.
treatments.name: Administration of Anticonvulsants
treatments.notes: This is necessary if the cat exhibits severe neurological signs, such as convulsions, which are documented effects of the plant's toxins.
